extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents), OED counsel, and adjudicators in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures for initiating, adjudicating, and imposing discipline (suspension/exclusion) on practitioners before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, including procedural rules, definitions of misconduct, factors for sanctions, and reinstatement requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO disciplinary authority and governing procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has the exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admission to practice before it and to suspend or exclude practitioners; this authority flows from 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and 35 U.S.C. § 32. Disciplinary hearings are conducted under the USPTO's procedural rules at 37 C.F.R. part 11, subpart C, and with section 7 of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 556, by appointed hearing officers (ALJs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statutory and regulatory bases for jurisdiction and procedure; indicates hearings are by hearing officer appointed under applicable interagency authorizations (e.g., HUD ALJs authorized to hear USPTO cases under an Interagency Agreement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express statutory/regulatory citation: 37 C.F.R. § 11.49; directs decisionmakers to apply clear-and-convincing standard when evaluating alleged misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to timely file an answer — admission and default judgment (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural consequence: non-answering respondent is deemed to have admitted allegations; OED may move for default judgment and the court may enter default and sanctions on that basis (illustrated by prior cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct — criminal acts reflecting adversely on honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to commit a criminal act that reflects adversely on the practitioner's honesty, trustworthiness or fitness as a practitioner in other respects (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied here to a felony Sherman Act conspiracy conviction (price-fixing/allocation) as conduct reflecting adversely on fitness; note also § 11.804(i) (engage in other conduct that adversely reflects) but the same conduct should not be relitigated under § 11.804(i) if it already violates other subsections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining appropriate sanction (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining an appropriate sanction, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's conduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers should analyze each of the four enumerated factors and may consult ABA STANDARDS and prior USPTO decisions to weigh severity; the Court applied these factors to conclude exclusion was warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (ABA STANDARDS § 9.22 examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors identified by the ABA STANDARDS (cited by the OED Director) include, for example, a dishonest or selfish motive and substantial experience in the practice of law (STANDARDS § 9.22(b) and (i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such aggravating factors warrant a more severe sanction; the decision found financial/personal gain and nearly 20 years' experience as aggravating in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (ABA STANDARDS §§ 9.31–9.32 examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors under the ABA STANDARDS are considerations that may justify a reduction in discipline; one example noted is the absence of a prior disciplinary record (STANDARDS § 9.32(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigating factors should be weighed against aggravating factors and injury; in this case the absence of prior discipline was given little weight given the nature and consequences of the misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of legal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of legal discipline is not to punish but to protect the public and the administration of justice from lawyers who have not or are unlikely to properly discharge their professional duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle (cited from ABA STANDARDS and case law) should guide selection of sanctions to protect public confidence and the integrity of the profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of culpable mental state (intentional/knowing vs. negligent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting intentionally or knowingly constitutes the most culpable mental state; where an offense (e.g., Sherman Act §1 conspiracy) requires an agreement, that demonstrates an intentional and knowing state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law may treat a conviction for an offense with an intent element as conclusive proof of intent for disciplinary purposes (citations provided). Decisionmakers should examine statutory elements and case law to infer mental state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of injury — actual or potential harm to public or clients
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's conduct is a key sanction factor; harm to the public (e.g., unreasonably restraining trade, driving up pharmaceutical prices) is relevant even if no client's interests were compromised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should consider both direct client injury and broader public/systemic harms when weighing sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations during suspension/exclusion and reinstatement prerequisites (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended or excluded practitioner is obligated to comply with the provisions of 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 during suspension/exclusion. An excluded or suspended practitioner who has violated any provision of § 11.58 shall not be eligible for reinstatement until a continuous period of time in compliance with § 11.58 equal to the period of suspension or exclusion has elapsed (37 C.F.R. § 11.60(c)). An excluded practitioner is eligible to apply for reinstatement no earlier than five years from the effective date of the exclusion (37 C.F.R. § 11.60(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must, e.g., submit required affidavits/declarations of compliance (see § 11.58(b)(2)); failure to comply may delay eligibility for reinstatement even if the exclusion's effective date is applied nunc pro tunc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim suspension, limited recognition period, and compliance documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An interim suspension order may grant limited recognition to practice for a short period (example: 30 days) to facilitate compliance with § 11.58(b). The practitioner is required to submit an affidavit or declaration of compliance as required by 37 C.F.R. § 11.58(b)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to submit required compliance documentation is a basis for finding noncompliance with suspension/exclusion obligations; courts may note absence of such affidavits when determining effective dates and reinsatement eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retroactive (nunc pro tunc) effective dates and continuing compliance obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may apply an exclusion nunc pro tunc (retroactively) to a prior suspension date, but applying an exclusion retroactively does not obviate the practitioner's duty to comply with 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when a retroactive effective date is granted (and unopposed by OED), the practitioner remains obligated to meet the explicit compliance requirements for suspension/exclusion and for reinstatement periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and scope of exclusion; appeals and required notices
rubrics_metrics.description: An order of exclusion bars the practitioner from practice before the USPTO in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters; excluded practitioners have appeal rights (either party may file an appeal to the USPTO Director within 30 days under 37 C.F.R. § 11.55).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orders include notices directing respondents to 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 regarding responsibilities and inform them of appeal timelines and reinstatement prerequisites; exclusion usually precludes practice and sets earliest reinstatement dates (e.g., five years).
